body:
Santorini is famous for things that look dramatic.

The caldera.

The cliffs.

The sunsets.

The black beaches.

Tomato fritters are not dramatic.

They are messy.

Rustic.

Fried.

And probably one of the most honest foods on the island.

They are called **ntomatokeftedes** — tomato fritters.

And the reason they matter is not because somebody invented a clever recipe.

It is because Santorini grows a very unusual tomato.

## Short answer

Ntomatokeftedes are traditional Santorini fritters made from chopped local tomatoes mixed with herbs, onion and flour, then fried until crisp outside and soft inside.

They are one of the island’s signature dishes.

The important part is the tomato.

Santorini’s small local tomato is dry-farmed in volcanic soil and has Protected Designation of Origin status.

That gives it the concentrated flavour that makes these fritters taste different from versions made elsewhere.

## A tomato that learned to survive without much water

Santorini is dry.

Very dry.

There are no lush green fields covering the island.

Rainfall is limited, summer heat is intense, and the volcanic soil does not look especially generous.

And yet tomatoes grow here.

The local variety developed under these harsh conditions.

Small fruit.

Thick skin.

Concentrated flavour.

Less water.

That last part matters enormously for frying.

A watery tomato produces a loose batter and soggy fritters.

A dense, intensely flavoured tomato gives you something much better.

That is one reason ntomatokeftedes became so closely associated with Santorini.

## The tomato itself is protected

The local product is known as **Tomataki Santorinis — Τοματάκι Σαντορίνης**.

It has PDO status.

That means the name is protected and tied to the geographical area and local production methods.

The official product specification describes it as a local small-fruited ecotype grown on Santorini.

This is not just marketing language.

The tomato is part of the agricultural identity of the island.

Visit Greece also lists tomatoes among Santorini’s defining crops, alongside vines and fava.

## The recipe looks almost too simple

There is no single sacred version.

That is worth saying immediately.

Some recipes use mint.

Others parsley.

Some include oregano.

Some add cheese.

Some add egg.

Some do not.

The core idea is simple:

* chopped tomatoes
* onion
* herbs
* flour
* salt and pepper
* olive oil for frying

The mixture should be thick enough to spoon into hot oil.

Then the fritters are fried until crisp and deeply golden around the edges.

Inside, they stay soft and almost jammy.

That contrast is the whole point.

## Why they are not just "tomato pancakes"

The word *keftedes* usually makes people think of meatballs.

But in Greek cooking, the idea is broader.

You also find zucchini fritters, chickpea fritters and other vegetable-based versions.

Ntomatokeftedes belong to that family.

They are not breakfast pancakes.

They are closer to a rustic vegetable fritter.

Crisp.

Savory.

Herby.

Best eaten hot.

And dangerous if the kitchen keeps sending out another plate.

## Santorini once had a tomato industry

This is the part many visitors do not know.

Tomatoes were not just something grown in a few gardens.

They became an important agricultural and industrial product.

By the middle of the 20th century, Santorini had several tomato-processing factories producing paste and canned products.

The Tomato Industrial Museum in Vlychada preserves this history inside a former processing factory.

The Nomikos family began producing tomato paste on Santorini in 1915.

A major factory opened in Vlychada in 1945.

At the industry’s peak, nine tomato factories were operating on the island.

Then tourism changed the economy.

Tomato cultivation shrank.

The Vlychada factory eventually closed in 1981.

Today it is a museum.

That story completely changes how I think about a plate of tomato fritters.

They are not just a restaurant snack.

They belong to an agricultural world that once employed families across the island.

## Why tourism nearly changed the tomato story

Santorini became more valuable as a destination than as farmland.

That sounds obvious now.

But it transformed the island.

Agricultural land declined.

Labour moved toward tourism.

Traditional crops became harder to maintain.

The tomato survived, but in a very different economic environment.

That is one reason local products like Santorini tomato, fava and wine matter.

They preserve an older version of the island underneath the hotels, terraces and infinity pools.

## What should good ntomatokeftedes taste like?

Not oily.

That is the first thing.

A good fritter should be crisp around the edges without feeling heavy.

Inside, the tomato should stay soft and juicy.

You should taste tomato first.

Then herbs.

Then onion.

The best versions have that slight sweet-acidic tomato intensity that makes you immediately understand why ordinary supermarket tomatoes would not produce the same result.

The fritters are often served with yoghurt or a creamy cheese-based dip.

But honestly, if the tomatoes are good enough, they do not need much.

## Where I would try them

I would not obsess over finding the “number one” tomato fritter on Santorini.

This is exactly the kind of dish where restaurant rankings become silly.

I would look for three things instead:

* a menu that clearly mentions Santorini tomato
* a kitchen serving local dishes rather than generic Greek greatest hits
* fritters cooked to order rather than sitting under heat lamps

If a place also serves local fava, white aubergine, capers and chloro cheese, that is usually a good sign that the kitchen is paying attention to Santorini ingredients.

## Want to understand the tomato properly?

Go to Vlychada.

The **Tomato Industrial Museum D. Nomikos** is housed in the old factory that operated there from 1945 until 1981.

It explains how Santorini tomatoes were cultivated, processed and turned into paste and canned products.

The museum still preserves machinery, factory documents, old tools and workers’ stories.

You even learn how important tomato production once was to the island economy.

It is one of those small museums that makes an ordinary food suddenly feel historical.

## And yes, you can learn to make them

Several cooking classes on Santorini include ntomatokeftedes.

That makes sense.

They are simple enough for visitors to prepare, but specific enough to teach something about the island.

Recent cooking-class reviews repeatedly mention tomato fritters as one of the dishes guests enjoy most.

Some farm-based classes also explain the history of tomato cultivation on Santorini before cooking.

That is the version I would choose.

Not because I need somebody to teach me how to fry batter.

Because I want the tomato story first.

## Are they vegetarian?

Usually, yes.

But do not assume.

Some recipes include egg.

Some include cheese.

Some restaurants serve them with dairy-based sauce.

If you are vegan or avoiding specific ingredients, ask.

The traditional idea is vegetable-based.

The exact recipe is not universal.

## Dan’s note

I like foods like this.

They are not trying to impress anyone.

A small tomato grows in difficult soil.

Someone chops it.

Adds onion and herbs.

Mixes in enough flour to hold everything together.

Then drops it into hot oil.

That is it.

But suddenly the whole island is in the plate.

Dry earth.

Strong sun.

Tomatoes that had to become intense because they had almost no water.

A farming industry that nearly disappeared.

And a dish that survived because it was too good to lose.

If I saw ntomatokeftedes on a Santorini menu, I would order them before almost anything else.

Preferably hot.

And definitely not just one.
hero_alt: Freshly fried Santorini tomato fritters made with local cherry tomatoes, herbs and flour, served warm with the volcanic landscape of the island in mind.
subtitle: Crisp outside, soft inside and built around Santorini’s tiny PDO tomatoes, ntomatokeftedes are one of the island’s simplest dishes — and one of the best ways to understand its dry volcanic landscape.
title: Santorini’s Tomato Fritters: Why Ntomatokeftedes Taste Different Here
